period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, reign of Menkaure, c. 2500 BC
summary: Three little pyramids in a row: one true pyramid and two step pyramids that never got their smooth casing.
look: South of Menkaure's pyramid stand three small pyramids in an east-west line. The eastern one, G3a, is a true pyramid, originally about 28 m high; the other two are four-stepped and uncased. From their south side the three great pyramids rise behind them.
story: Each of these little pyramids had its own mud-brick temple on its east face. George Reisner attributed the eastern and largest, G3a, to Menkaure's queen Khamerernebty II, though that is still debated; Mark Lehner thinks it may have been a 'ka pyramid' for the king's spirit. In the middle one, G3b, Howard Vyse found a plain granite sarcophagus holding bones, including the jaw of what was probably a young woman, and a roof beam carries a quarry mark with Menkaure's name. The western one, G3c, was left unfinished inside. Vyse blamed its battered state on Napoleon's soldiers using it for target practice.
details: Eastern pyramid, G3a: a true pyramid, with red granite in its lowest course.
The two western ones: count the four steps of each, a rough core that never received its casing.
Walk round to the south side for the classic photo of small pyramids in front of the three giants.
fun_fact: Vyse blamed Napoleon's gunners for smashing the western pyramid. Nobody has ever proved it.
narration: These three small pyramids south of Menkaure's were built for the women of his family. The eastern one, the biggest, is a true pyramid, once about 28 metres high, with red granite at its base. George Reisner gave it to Menkaure's queen Khamerernebty, though others think it held a statue of the king's spirit. The other two are step pyramids, four steps each, that never received their smooth casing. Inside the middle one, explorers found a granite sarcophagus with the bones of what was probably a young woman. And the battered western one, Howard Vyse claimed, was used by Napoleon's soldiers for target practice. From their south side, the three little pyramids line up in front of the giants.

period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, probably reign of Khafre, c. 2550 BC
summary: Carved from the bedrock, not built: a lion with a king's face, 73 m long, and still arguing with Egyptologists about whose face it is.
look: The Sphinx lies in a hollow quarried out of the plateau, facing east towards the sunrise: 73 m long from paws to tail and 20 m high. The head, cut from a harder layer of rock, is well preserved; the body, in softer layers, is deeply weathered and patched with masonry from ancient and modern repairs. Between the paws stands the granite Dream Stele.
story:
The Sphinx was not assembled from blocks: the builders quarried away the rock around a knoll and left a lion with a human head. The stone they removed went into the temple in front of it. Most Egyptologists think it was made for Khafre, because it sits beside his valley temple and causeway, but no inscription of his time says so. Rainer Stadelmann argued for Khufu; Vassil Dobrev suggested Khufu's son Djedefre. The fringe idea that rain erosion makes it thousands of years older is rejected by mainstream scholars.

We do not know what its makers called it. A thousand years later it was worshipped as Horemakhet, 'Horus in the Horizon'. 'Sphinx' is a Greek name given some 2,000 years after it was carved, borrowed from the monster of Thebes who strangled those who failed her riddle. In Arabic it is Abu el-Hol, 'father of terror'.

The nose was not shot off by Napoleon's soldiers: Frederic Norden's drawings from 1737 already show it missing, and chisel marks show it was deliberately pried off. The historian al-Maqrizi blamed a Sufi, Muhammad Sa'im al-Dahr, who attacked the face in 1378 because peasants made offerings to it. Fragments of a carved beard were found between the paws; one is in the British Museum. Traces of red paint survive on the face.

Sand has buried it to the shoulders again and again. Thutmose IV cleared it around 1400 BC, the Romans cleared it under Nero, Giovanni Battista Caviglia uncovered the chest in 1817, and Emile Baraize cleared the sand in 1926.
details: The face: traces of red paint survive; Pliny wrote that it was painted red out of reverence.
The nose: look for the marks of chisels driven in at the bridge and below the nostril.
The body: soft layered rock eroded into horizontal bands; the paws and flanks are cased in repair blocks.
Between the paws: the granite Dream Stele of Thutmose IV.
The neck: in 1931 engineers added a concrete collar after part of the headdress fell in 1926.
fun_fact: European travellers from the 16th to the 19th century often described the Sphinx as a woman, with a female face, neck and breast.
narration: In front of you is the Great Sphinx, a lion with a king's head, 73 metres long and 20 metres high, facing the sunrise. It was not built from blocks. The builders quarried the plateau away around a knob of rock and carved what was left, then used the stone they removed for the temple in front. Most Egyptologists think the face is Khafre's, about 4,500 years old, because it sits beside his valley temple, but no inscription of his time says so, and some argue for his father Khufu or his brother Djedefre. We do not know what its makers called it. A thousand years later it was worshipped as Horemakhet, Horus in the Horizon. Sphinx is a Greek name, borrowed from the monster of Thebes who strangled travellers who failed her riddle. And no, Napoleon's soldiers did not shoot off the nose. A drawing from 1737 already shows it missing, and the historian al-Maqrizi blamed a Sufi zealot who attacked the face in 1378, angry that farmers were making offerings to it. Sand has buried the Sphinx up to its shoulders again and again, and every clearance, by a pharaoh, a Roman emperor and modern archaeologists, has been a rescue. Now look closely at the face: at the bridge of the nose and below the nostril you can see where chisels were hammered in to pry it off.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Thutmose IV, c. 1401 BC
summary: A prince naps in the Sphinx's shadow and dreams that the god will make him king if he clears away the sand.
look: Between the Sphinx's front paws stands a granite slab about 3.6 m high, weighing about 15 tonnes. In the rounded scene at the top, Thutmose IV appears twice, making offerings to a sphinx on a high pedestal; below are lines of text, broken off about halfway down. It formed the back wall of a small open-air chapel between the paws.
story:
Thutmose IV set this stone up in the first year of his reign; the text is dated year 1, third month of the flood season, day 19. As a young prince, it says, he went hunting near Memphis with two companions, shooting at targets and chasing lions. At noon he lay down in the shadow of the great god and fell asleep. In a dream the Sphinx, calling himself Horemakhet-Khepri-Ra-Atum, spoke to him as a father to a son, promised him the crowns of Upper and Lower Egypt, and complained that the desert sand had reached him. The rest is lost, but the message is clear: clear my sand and you will be king.

Why would a prince need a god's promise? Selim Hassan suggested Thutmose was not the heir and pushed aside older brothers, whose names were erased on other stelae here. Betsy Bryan points out that divine choice was a standard theme of the dynasty, so the case is unproven.

The stone is recycled: pivot sockets on its back show it was a door lintel from Khafre's mortuary temple. Caviglia's diggers uncovered it in 1818.
details: The lunette at the top: Thutmose IV appears twice, offering to the Sphinx on its pedestal.
The broken lower half: about half the inscription is lost below the big crack.
Above the stele: the Sphinx's chest, where fragments of its stone beard were found.
fun_fact: Thomas Young, Champollion's great rival in the race to decipher hieroglyphs, tried to restore a broken cartouche on this stone as Khafre's name.
narration: Between the Sphinx's paws stands a granite slab 3.6 metres high: the Dream Stele of Thutmose IV, set up around 1401 BC, more than a thousand years after the Sphinx was carved. Its story is irresistible. A young prince goes hunting in the desert with two companions. At noon he lies down in the shadow of the Sphinx and falls asleep. In a dream the god speaks to him like a father to a son, promises him the crowns of Egypt, and complains that the sand is choking him. Clear my sand, and you will be king. Thutmose did become king, and the sand was cleared. Was he the rightful heir? Some Egyptologists think he pushed older brothers aside and needed a god's endorsement. Others say divine choice was a standard royal theme. Either way, the stone itself was recycled: it is a door lintel taken from Khafre's temple up the hill. Look at the top of the stele: Thutmose appears twice, making offerings to a sphinx on a tall pedestal.

period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, probably reign of Khafre, c. 2550 BC
summary: A temple built from the Sphinx's own quarry, with a sanctuary to the east and one to the west, and never finished.
look: Directly in front of the Sphinx, just north of Khafre's valley temple, lie the low walls of a temple of enormous limestone blocks around a central court. It is usually seen from outside and above, from the viewing terrace.
story: No inscription names its builder, but its plan resembles Khafre's temples, and most Egyptologists give it to him. Its core blocks came from the hollow cut around the Sphinx as the statue was carved. Around the open court stood 24 pillars, apparently each with a statue of the king. At the east and west were two sanctuaries. One theory, from the architect Herbert Ricke, gives it a solar meaning: one sanctuary for the rising sun, one for the setting sun, and 24 pillars for the hours of day and night. The temple was never finished, and no reliefs or texts were carved.
details: From the terrace: the rectangle of the central court, with the bases of its pillars.
The size of the core blocks: they were cut from the hollow around the Sphinx.
East and west ends: the two recesses read as sanctuaries for sunrise and sunset.
fun_fact: Both the temple and the Sphinx's enclosure were left unfinished: at some point the quarrymen simply stopped.
narration: The low walls right in front of the Sphinx belong to the Sphinx Temple, probably built under Khafre, though no inscription says so. Its huge limestone blocks were cut from the hollow around the Sphinx itself, so in a sense the temple and the statue are made from the same hole. Around an open court stood 24 pillars, probably each with a statue of the king. At the east and west ends were two sanctuaries. One theory says they greeted the rising and the setting sun, and that the 24 pillars stood for the hours of day and night. The temple was never finished and never inscribed. Look down at the courtyard and try to pick out the line of pillar bases around it.

period: Old Kingdom, end of Fourth Dynasty to early Fifth Dynasty, c. 2500 BC
summary: A queen with a title so ambiguous it might make her a king: her huge two-step tomb is nicknamed the fourth pyramid of Giza.
look: Near Menkaure's valley temple, north of his causeway, rises a huge two-stepped block. The lower step, about 45 m square and 10 m high, is bedrock left standing by the quarrymen; the upper step, built over its western half, brings it to 17.5 m.
story: Khentkawes I lived at the hinge between the Fourth and Fifth Dynasties. Her title, carved on the red granite doorjambs of her chapel, can be read two ways: 'mother of two kings of Upper and Lower Egypt', or 'king of Upper and Lower Egypt and mother of the king of Upper and Lower Egypt'. She was shown with a vulture crown and a ritual beard. Her sons may have been Shepseskaf and Userkaf, but nobody knows. Selim Hassan identified her in 1932. Beside her tomb he found a planned L-shaped town of mud-brick houses for the priests of her cult, with granaries and a large water tank.
details: The lower step: bedrock left standing while the stone around it was quarried for the pyramids.
The upper step: built on the western half only, slightly vaulted on top.
The south-east corner: the chapel entrance, where her title was carved on red granite jambs.
fun_fact: Early explorers took this for an unfinished pyramid of King Shepseskaf. Only in 1932 did the granite doorjambs reveal it belonged to a woman.
narration: This huge two stepped block near Menkaure's valley temple is sometimes called the fourth pyramid of Giza. It is the tomb of Queen Khentkawes, who lived as the Fourth Dynasty gave way to the Fifth, about 2500 BC. The lower step is bedrock, left standing while the builders quarried the stone around it. Her title, carved on the granite doorway of her chapel, can be read in two ways: mother of two kings of Egypt, or king of Egypt and mother of a king. She is shown wearing a royal beard. Was she a regent, a king, or a royal mother? Nobody knows. Beside the tomb, archaeologists found a small planned town where her priests lived. Look for the smaller second step, built on the western half only.

period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, c. 2580-2470 BC
summary: Not slaves: bakers, brewers, masons and haulers who ate beef, had their broken bones set, and were buried with honour beside the pyramids.
look: South-east of the Sphinx and Menkaure's valley temple runs a long stone wall, the Wall of the Crow, Heit el-Ghurab in Arabic. Beyond it lay the town archaeologists call the Lost City of the Pyramid Builders, and on the slope above it the workers' cemetery. Neither is normally on the tourist route, but from the high ground you can look over where they lived.
story:
Herodotus was told that 100,000 men built the Great Pyramid in three-month shifts. Later writers and Hollywood turned them into slaves under the whip. The evidence on the ground tells another story.

From the late 1980s Mark Lehner's team excavated a planned town beyond the Wall of the Crow, dating to the reigns of Khafre and Menkaure. It has long galleries like barracks, bakeries, breweries, kitchens and a copper workshop. The rubbish heaps are full of bones of cattle, sheep, goats and fish: people here ate meat. Later finds, including a harbour, suggest that many residents were sailors and soldiers, and Lehner thinks many builders may have camped on the construction sites themselves.

In 1990, the story goes, a horse stumbled over a mud-brick wall on the slope above. Zahi Hawass's team uncovered a cemetery of workmen and their overseers: small tombs, some with tiny pyramids or false doors, with jars of bread and beer for the afterlife. The skeletons show hard lives, with worn spines and arthritis from heavy loads, but also healed fractures that someone had set. Slaves were not buried with honour in the shadow of the king's tomb.

The workforce was organised like a sports league. Graffiti name gangs such as 'Friends of Khufu' and 'Drunkards of Menkaure', divided into units Egyptologists call by the Greek word phyles, and smaller groups of 20 to 40 men. Modern estimates put the total at 20,000 to 30,000 people, many probably serving a few months of labour owed to the state.
details: The long stone wall south-east of the Sphinx: the Wall of the Crow, between the sacred plateau and the town.
The slope above the wall: the workers' cemetery, with small mud-brick tombs and miniature pyramids.
On any core block near you: rough faces and tool marks, real hours of human work.
In the Great Pyramid's relieving chambers, not visitable, gang names in red paint: the workers' own signatures.
fun_fact: One gang chose to call itself the 'Drunkards of Menkaure'. Beer was part of the daily ration, so the name may be less of a joke than it sounds.
narration: Who built the pyramids? Not slaves. That image comes from Greek writers and Hollywood, not from the evidence. Look south-east, beyond the long stone wall known as the Wall of the Crow. There, from the late 1980s, Mark Lehner's team uncovered a planned town from the time of Khafre and Menkaure: long barracks, bakeries, breweries, kitchens and a copper workshop. The rubbish heaps are full of bones of cattle, sheep, goats and fish. The people who lived here ate meat, and plenty of it. Then in 1990, the story goes, a horse stumbled over a mud brick wall on the slope above, and Zahi Hawass's team found a cemetery of workers and their foremen. Small tombs, some with tiny pyramids of their own, jars of bread and beer for the afterlife, and skeletons with worn backs and healed broken bones. Someone had set those fractures and cared for the injured. The crews were organised like sports teams, with names painted on the blocks: Friends of Khufu, and one gang that called itself the Drunkards of Menkaure. Modern estimates suggest 20,000 to 30,000 people, many serving a few months of labour owed to the king, a tax paid in sweat. Before you move on, look towards that wall in the distance and imagine the smoke from the bakeries rising behind it.

period: Old Kingdom, Third to Fourth Dynasty, c. 2670-2500 BC
summary: Copper chisels, wet sand, boats, ramps and a great deal of bread: how a Bronze Age state moved millions of tonnes of stone.
look: The evidence is all around you: the quarry hollows south of the Great Pyramid and around the Sphinx, where core blocks were cut; the rough, tool-marked faces of the blocks; the Aswan granite of the temples. The fine white casing came from Tura, across the river.
story:
Start with the stone. Most core blocks were quarried right here, from fossil-rich local limestone. Workers cut channels around each block with chisels of arsenical copper, then split it free with wedges and levers; in a modern experiment at a quarry of Khufu's time, four men with replica tools cut a 2.5-tonne block in four days. Granite was too hard for copper. It was pounded with balls of dolerite and sawn or drilled using quartz sand as an abrasive. Casing limestone crossed the Nile by boat from Tura, and granite came more than 900 km from Aswan.

Moving it: on wooden sledges over wetted ground. A Middle Kingdom tomb painting shows 172 men dragging a colossal statue on a sledge while a man pours water in front, and in 2014 physicists in Amsterdam showed that the right amount of water roughly halves the pulling force on sand. Boats did the long hauls, along canals and a lost branch of the Nile that once ran close to Giza.

Lifting it: the honest answer is that nobody is sure. Ramps are the favourite, but a single straight ramp would have been enormous, so scholars propose zigzag ramps, ramps spiralling round the faces, or Jean-Pierre Houdin's ramp inside the pyramid. In 2018 a team at the Hatnub alabaster quarry found a steep ramp flanked by stairs and post-holes for ropes, used on slopes of 20 percent or more and dating at least to Khufu's time. Levers, as Herodotus described, probably did the final placing.

And aliens? Everything points to people: quarry marks, unfinished blocks, early pyramids that failed and taught lessons, workers' graffiti, their town, and Merer's logbook.
details: South of the Great Pyramid: the old quarry where most of its core blocks were cut.
On the core blocks: fossil shells, tool marks, and rough faces once hidden by the casing.
Khafre's valley temple: Aswan granite, shaped by pounding and sawing with sand.
Menkaure's pyramid: granite casing left rough, showing that the faces were smoothed after the blocks were set.
The Great Pyramid's base: level to within about 2 cm across 230 m.
fun_fact: In 1992 Mark Lehner and stonemason Roger Hopkins built a 6 m pyramid of 186 stones for a TV documentary in three weeks. Copper tools worked, if a crew kept resharpening them.
narration: How do you build a mountain without pulleys or iron tools? With copper, water, rope, boats and a lot of organised people. Most of the stone was quarried right here, just south of the Great Pyramid. Workers cut channels around each block with copper chisels and split it free with wooden wedges. In a modern test, four men with replica tools cut a 2.5 tonne block in four days. Hard granite was pounded with balls of dolerite and sawn with sand. The fine white casing came by boat from Tura across the river, and the granite from Aswan, more than 900 kilometres upstream, along a branch of the Nile that once ran close to the plateau. Over land, blocks were dragged on wooden sledges. An Egyptian tomb painting shows a man pouring water in front of a sledge, and physicists have shown that wet sand roughly halves the pulling force. Lifting them is still argued over. Straight ramps, zigzag ramps, spiral ramps and even a ramp inside the pyramid all have their champions, and in 2018 archaeologists found a steep ramp with stairs and post holes at an alabaster quarry, dating back at least to Khufu's time. Levers probably did the final placing. And aliens? Everything points to people: quarry marks, workers' graffiti, their town, their tombs, and early pyramids that failed. Now look at any core block near you and find the marks of their tools.

period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, late in Khufu's reign, c. 2560 BC
summary: The oldest inscribed papyri ever found are a foreman's logbook: Merer and his 40 boatmen shipping limestone to the Great Pyramid.
look: There is nothing to see on the plateau itself: the papyri were found in 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea, and parts have been displayed in Cairo, so trust the labels for which museum. Stand at the foot of the Great Pyramid and look east, over the modern town, to where Khufu's harbour received Merer's boats.
story:
In 2013 a French team led by Pierre Tallet and Gregory Marouard was excavating Wadi al-Jarf, a harbour of Khufu's time on the Red Sea coast. Buried in front of the caves where boats were stored, they found papyrus rolls: the oldest inscribed papyri known.

The best preserved belong to an inspector called Merer, who commanded about 40 boatmen. Under headings for month and season, he logged their work day by day, in the 26th or 27th year of Khufu's reign. From July to November they shipped white limestone from the Tura quarries to 'Akhet Khufu', the Horizon of Khufu, the Great Pyramid's ancient name. Every ten days or so they made two or three round trips, carrying perhaps 30 blocks of 2 to 3 tonnes each, about 200 blocks a month. Tallet thinks the stone was for the casing. It was received at a harbour at Giza, Ra-shi-Khufu, under the noble Ankhhaf, Khufu's half-brother.

The diary turns the pyramid into what it was: a logistics project of canals, harbours, rations and schedules. Why the archive ended up at a Red Sea port is not certain; the crew may simply have been sent there next.
details: Foot of the north face: surviving Tura casing blocks, the kind of stone Merer's crew delivered.
Look east over the town: Khufu's harbour, Ra-shi-Khufu, lay down there, under modern Giza.
Eastern Cemetery: Ankhhaf, Merer's boss, has the largest mastaba there, G7510.
If you see the papyri in Cairo: each entry starts with month and season, then the days follow.
fun_fact: The oldest inscribed papyri in the world are not poetry or scripture. They are, essentially, a timesheet.
narration: Imagine finding the logbook of a man who helped build the Great Pyramid. In 2013 French archaeologists did exactly that, at Wadi al-Jarf, a harbour of Khufu's time on the Red Sea. Buried in front of caves used to store boats were the oldest inscribed papyri ever found. The best preserved belong to an inspector called Merer, who commanded about 40 boatmen near the end of Khufu's reign. Day by day he recorded their work: sailing to the Tura quarries across the river, loading fine white limestone, and shipping it to Akhet Khufu, the Horizon of Khufu, which is what the Egyptians called this pyramid. Every ten days or so they made two or three round trips, carrying perhaps 30 blocks of 2 to 3 tonnes each. The stone was received at a harbour at Giza run by the noble Ankhhaf, Khufu's half brother. No slaves, no mysteries: canals, schedules, rations and paperwork. Look down at the smooth casing blocks at the foot of the north face: stone like this came here on Merer's boats.

period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, reign of Khufu, c. 2560 BC
summary: Five boat pits surround the Great Pyramid, and two of them held complete cedar ships, dismantled and sealed for 4,500 years.
look: On the east side of the Great Pyramid, near the black basalt paving of the vanished mortuary temple, are long boat-shaped trenches cut into the rock, pointed at both ends and now empty. On the south side lay two long rectangular pits, once covered by limestone slabs of up to 15 tonnes, which held the two dismantled ships.
story:
Khufu was given five boat pits: three boat-shaped ones on the east, found empty, and two rectangular ones on the south. In May 1954 Kamal el-Mallakh, clearing debris along the south side, found the slabs sealing the first. When he broke through, it is said, he smelled cedar. Inside lay 1,224 pieces of a ship, laid out in logical order. Many cover blocks bore the name of Djedefre, Khufu's son and successor, who must have carried out the burial.

The restorer Ahmed Youssef Moustafa spent more than a decade working out how the pieces fitted, guided by ancient models and modern Nile boatyards. The result is a cedar ship about 43.5 m long, its planks lashed with rope. From 1982 it stood in a museum beside the pit; in August 2021 it moved to the Grand Egyptian Museum, where you saw it on the 11th.

The second southern pit was examined with a camera in 1987 and excavated from about 2010 by a Japanese and Egyptian team from Waseda University; its timbers have been restored at the GEM. What the ships were for is still argued: a solar barque to sail with the sun god, or the barge that carried the king's body to Giza.
details: East side, near the basalt paving: the empty boat-shaped pits, pointed at both ends like a hull.
The basalt paving itself: almost all that survives of Khufu's mortuary temple.
South side: the two long rectangular pits that held the dismantled ships.
Graffiti in the second pit named Khufu four times and Djedefre eleven times, in red and black ink.
fun_fact: The first ship was buried as a flat-pack kit of 1,224 pieces in logical order, perhaps the oldest self-assembly instructions in history.
narration: Around the Great Pyramid the rock is cut with long pits shaped like boats. Khufu had five. The boat shaped ones on the east were found empty, but two long rectangular pits on the south side held real ships. In May 1954 the archaeologist Kamal el-Mallakh broke through the slabs sealing the first one, and, the story goes, the smell of cedar wood rose out of the dark. Inside lay 1,224 pieces of a dismantled ship, stacked in order like a flat pack kit. Many of the cover blocks carried the name of Djedefre, Khufu's son, who must have buried it. The restorer Ahmed Youssef Moustafa spent more than ten years working out how it fitted together. The finished ship, about 43 metres of cedar, is the one you saw at the Grand Egyptian Museum on the 11th, along with the second ship, excavated by a Japanese and Egyptian team. Were they for the king's funeral, or to sail across the sky with the sun god? Nobody knows. Look for an empty pit on the east side, pointed at both ends like a hull.

summary: The postcard view: the Giza pyramids lined up across the desert, best in the warm light of late afternoon.
look: You are on the high desert south-west of Menkaure's pyramid, looking north-east. Menkaure's three small queens' pyramids sit in front, then Menkaure's, Khafre's and Khufu's pyramids step away diagonally behind, with Cairo's towers beyond.
story:
Why do they line up like this? Each king built a little south-west of his father, along the edge of the plateau, so the three pyramids fall roughly on a diagonal. In theory you can count nine: the three kings, Menkaure's three queens in front, and Khufu's three queens. In practice Khufu's queens hide behind the Great Pyramid, so six are easy and the rest are a matter of faith.

The recent revamp of the plateau put a restaurant here, the 9 Pyramids Lounge. The camel and horse owners gather here too. If you want a ride, agree the total price, the route, the time and the way back before you climb on, and pay at the end. If not, a smile and 'la shukran' is enough.
details: Front left: Menkaure's queens, one true pyramid and two step pyramids.
Top of Khafre's pyramid: the surviving cap of casing catches the light.
Late afternoon: the sun behind you lights the faces you see; mornings are backlit and hazy.
Before any ride: agree price, route and return, and pay at the end.
fun_fact: Nine pyramids is the official count, but from this spot you would need X-ray vision to see Khufu's three queens.
narration: This is the postcard view. You are on the high desert south-west of the pyramids, looking north-east, and the whole family is lined up for you. In front are the three little pyramids of Menkaure's queens. Behind them, stepping away on a diagonal, come Menkaure's pyramid, then Khafre's with its cap of casing, and finally the Great Pyramid of Khufu. The line is no accident: each king built a little south-west of his father, along the edge of the plateau. People call this the nine pyramids view, but Khufu's three queens hide behind his pyramid, so count six and take the other three on trust. The light is best in the late afternoon, when the sun is behind you and the stone turns gold. This is also the camel stop. If you want a ride, agree the total price, the route, the time and the way back before you climb on, and pay at the end. If not, smile, say la shukran, and walk on. Now look at the top of Khafre's pyramid and watch the old casing catch the light.

period: Old Kingdom, Third to Sixth Dynasty, c. 2670-2180 BC
summary: A pyramid is a mound of creation, a sunbeam in stone and a launch ramp to the stars, all in one shape.
look: Look at a pyramid face-on in sunlight. Many scholars think the slope echoed the rays of the sun slanting down through cloud, and the point recalled the benben, the first mound that rose from the waters. Notice too that the entrances at Giza are all on the north faces, towards the stars that never set.
story:
In the creation story of Heliopolis, the city the Greeks named 'Sun City', the world began as dark water called Nu. A mound rose from it, and the creator Atum settled on it: the benben. In the sun temple at Heliopolis a sacred stone of the same name caught the first rays of the sun, and a pyramid's capstone was called the benbenet. The Pyramid Texts say Atum rose up as the benben in the Mansion of the Bennu, the bird that probably inspired the Greek phoenix.

The pyramid was also a machine for the king's ascent, to join Ra in his boat and the circumpolar 'imperishable' stars of the north, which never set.

The shape came by trial and error. Djoser's step pyramid at Saqqara, around 2670 BC, stacked mastabas into a stairway. Sneferu, Khufu's father, built Meidum, which partly collapsed, then the Bent Pyramid, which changes angle halfway up, and finally the Red Pyramid, the first true pyramid completed. His son built the Great Pyramid.

After Giza, pyramids shrank. Fifth and Sixth Dynasty kings built smaller ones, but carved the Pyramid Texts inside. Middle Kingdom kings used mud-brick cores. All were robbed, and New Kingdom kings hid their tombs in the Valley of the Kings, under a peak shaped like a pyramid.
details: North faces: every Giza pyramid's entrance faces the stars that circle the pole.
Top of Khafre's pyramid: imagine a polished capstone, the benbenet, flashing in the first light.
The slope against the sky in late afternoon: the shape is thought to echo the sun's rays.
On the 21st, look up from the Valley of the Kings at the Qurn, the natural pyramid that replaced built ones.
fun_fact: The Bent Pyramid's ancient name was 'The Southern Shining Pyramid'. Pyramids were meant to dazzle, not just to be big.
narration: Why a pyramid? For the Egyptians the shape meant several things at once. In the creation story of Heliopolis, the city the Greeks called Sun City, the world began as dark water, and the first thing to appear was a mound of earth, where the creator god settled. A sacred stone called the benben, in the temple of the sun god Ra, recalled that first mound, and the capstone of a pyramid was called the benbenet. The sloping sides probably echoed the rays of the sun slanting down through cloud, a ramp for the king to climb to Ra. And the entrances face north, towards the stars that circle the pole and never set, the imperishable ones the king hoped to join. The shape was reached by trial and error: Djoser's step pyramid, then Khufu's father Sneferu, who built one that partly collapsed and one that changes angle halfway up. After Giza, pyramids shrank, and later kings hid their tombs in the Valley of the Kings instead, under a natural pyramid of rock. Find the entrance on the north face of the nearest pyramid: that was the door to the stars.
